## From promised payments to state-dependent cash flows

<div class="flow"><span><b>Option-free</b>Discount a fixed schedule</span><i>→</i><span><b>Embedded option</b>Model future rates and exercise</span><i>→</i><span><b>Price and risk</b>Value the resulting cash flows</span></div>

$$
P=\sum_t CF_tP(0,t)
$$

With a call or put, you must value the payments that remain after exercise.

## Our valuation steps

<div class="flow"><span><b>Yield spread</b>What does it mix together?</span><i>→</i><span><b>Static spread</b>Use the full spot curve</span><i>→</i><span><b>Rate lattice</b>Make exercise state dependent</span><i>→</i><span><b>OAS and risk</b>Reprice with the option</span></div>

## Traditional spread compresses the cash-flow schedule

$$
\text{Yield spread}=YTM_{\mathrm{bond}}-YTM_{\mathrm{Treasury}}
$$

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>One yield</h3><p>YTM summarizes many dated cash flows. Realizing it requires the relevant reinvestment assumptions.</p></div><div><h3>Several risks</h3><p>Credit, liquidity and embedded options all enter the spread.</p></div></div>

## Why a single spread can mislead

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Curve mismatch</h3><p>Different cash-flow timing and nonparallel yield curves can distort a same-maturity comparison.</p></div><div><h3>Changing cash flows</h3><p>An embedded option changes payments when rates change; YTM does not model exercise.</p></div></div>

## The quoted spread contains several components

A 150 bp quoted spread can combine 75 bp for credit, 25 bp for liquidity, and 50 bp for the embedded option.

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-spread-components.svg){.figure}


## Static spread uses every spot rate

$$
P=\sum_t\frac{CF_t}{(1+r_t+s)^t}
$$

<div class="flow"><span><b>Spot curve</b>Match each payment date</span><i>→</i><span><b>One spread</b>Add the same s at every date</span><i>→</i><span><b>Promised payments</b>Cash flows remain fixed</span></div>

## A constant spread shifts the spot curve

Add the same 80 bp to the spot rate at every maturity.

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-static-spread-curve.svg){.figure}


## Static-spread example: set up the payments

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Bond</h3><p>5 years; face $1,000; 6% annual coupon paid semiannually.</p></div><div><h3>Market</h3><p>Price $1,020; ten dated spot rates, from 2.0% to 4.3%.</p></div></div>

<div class="cash-timeline" data-times='["0", "0.5", "1", "\u2026", "4.5", "5"]' data-flows='["\u2212$1,020", "$30", "$30", "\u2026", "$30", "$1,030"]'></div>

Each half-year coupon is $1000(0.06)/2=30$; the final payment is $1000+30=1030$.

## Keep the discount convention consistent

| Time (years) | .5 | 1 | 1.5 | 2 | 2.5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Spot rate | 2.0% | 2.2% | 2.6% | 3.0% | 3.4% |

| Time (years) | 3 | 3.5 | 4 | 4.5 | 5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Spot rate | 3.8% | 4.0% | 4.1% | 4.2% | 4.3% |

Use **effective annual** spot rates. Payment $k$ arrives at $t_k=k/2$ years; use that time in the discount exponent.

## Solve for the spread, rather than averaging yields

$$
1020=\sum_{k=1}^{9}\frac{30}{(1+r_{k/2}+s)^{k/2}}+\frac{1030}{(1+0.043+s)^5}
$$

$$
s=0.01400712\approx140.07\text{ bp}
$$

Add $s=1.400712\%$ to each annual spot rate. The payments then have a present value of \$1,020. In basis points, $0.01400712\times10{,}000=140.07$.

## Price is nonlinear in the static spread

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-static-spread.svg){.figure}

Find the spread where the present-value curve crosses the market price of \$1,020.

## The issuer calls when refinancing becomes attractive

<div class="flow"><span><b>Rates fall</b>The old coupon is expensive</span><i>→</i><span><b>Issuer refinances</b>Redeem at the call price</span><i>→</i><span><b>Investor loses upside</b>Above-market coupons disappear</span></div>

When rates fall, the issuer can replace expensive debt with cheaper debt.

## Callability matters most in low-rate states

At a call date with a total payment of 100, compare the cost of continuing with 100. The issuer chooses the cheaper alternative.

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-callable-bond-economic-states.svg){.figure}


## The option has a price

$$
V_{\mathrm{callable}}=V_{\mathrm{straight}}-V_{\mathrm{call}}
$$

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>High yields</h3><p>Call unlikely; the bond behaves more like an option-free bond.</p></div><div><h3>Low yields</h3><p>Exercise becomes attractive; price appreciation slows and effective maturity shortens.</p></div></div>

## Yield to worst is a reporting convention

$$
YTW=\min\{YTM,\ YTC_1,\ YTC_2,\ldots\}
$$

Use the relevant permitted call dates. The minimum yield does not model the probability of exercise, future volatility or the full term structure.

## Separate the bond from the embedded option

$$
V_{\mathrm{callable}}=V_{\mathrm{straight}}-V_{\mathrm{call}}
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{putable}}=V_{\mathrm{straight}}+V_{\mathrm{put}}
$$

The issuer owns the call; the investor owns the put.

## The call option explains the missing upside

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-embedded-option-decomposition.svg){.figure}

The gap between the two bond values is the value of the issuer’s call. Use this sketch to see why the investor gives up upside.

## Value the final payoff, then work backward

<div class="flow"><span><b>Rate states</b>Construct future short rates</span><i>→</i><span><b>Maturity</b>Set terminal cash flows</span><i>→</i><span><b>Rollback</b>Discount risk-neutral continuation</span><i>→</i><span><b>Exercise</b>Apply the contract at each node</span></div>

## Time and rate states in a lattice

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-lattice-time-and-states.svg){.figure}

Read across for later dates. At one date, move up or down to compare rate states. At each node, decide whether the bond continues or the option is exercised.

## Backward induction reverses the direction of time

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-backward-induction-intuition.svg){.figure}

Start at maturity. Apply exercise where permitted, then discount the resulting values back one date.

## Three-year example: contract and assumptions

Consider this annual-pay bond:

| Contract | Rate model |
|---|---|
| Face value 100; annual coupon 8; maturity 3 years | Annual steps; risk-neutral up probability $p=0.5$ |
| First call date: year 2 | Initial short rate: 6% |
| Call at par: principal 100 + coupon 8 = total payment 108 | Year-1 rates: 5% and 9%; year-2 rates: 4%, 8%, and 12% |

We value the bond just before the current coupon. A call at year 2 pays principal 100 plus coupon 8. If the bond reaches year 3, maturity also pays 100 plus 8. Subtract the immediate coupon of 8 to get the ex-coupon purchase price at time zero.

## The short-rate lattice

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-simple-rate-lattice.svg){.figure}

Trace the two possible moves from each node. At year 3, the bond pays 108 in every state.

## Backward induction includes the current coupon

$$
H_{i,j}=\frac{pV_{i+1,j+1}+(1-p)V_{i+1,j}}{1+r_{i,j}}+CF_i
$$

Use $p$ for the risk-neutral up probability, $r_{i,j}$ for the node’s one-period short rate, and $CF_i$ for the current coupon.

Discount the two next-period values, then add the current coupon once.

## Exercise replaces continuation value

$$
V^{\mathrm{callable}}_{i,j}=\min\{H_{i,j},K_i\}
$$

$$
V^{\mathrm{putable}}_{i,j}=\max\{H_{i,j},K_i^{\mathrm{put}}\}
$$

Compare the hold value and the exercise payment on the same coupon-inclusive basis. Apply the rule only when the contract allows exercise.

## Choose the exercise action at each node

| Contract | Compare the hold value $H$ with the total exercise payment $K$ | Node value |
|---|---|---|
| Callable | If $H>K$, the issuer calls; otherwise, the bond continues | $\min(H,K)$ |
| Putable | If $H<K$, the investor puts; otherwise, the bond continues | $\max(H,K)$ |

Check the contract’s exercise dates before applying either rule. On other dates, keep the hold value.

## Step 1 — set the terminal payoff {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 3: start at maturity · gold nodes = values set now</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-terminal.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{3,j}=100+8=108\qquad\text{in every state}$$

Both bonds pay principal **100** plus coupon **8** at maturity. Set these final values before moving one year to the left.

## Step 2 — roll back to year 2 {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 3 → year 2 · gold nodes = hold values calculated now</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-year2.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$H_{2,j}=\frac{0.5(108)+0.5(108)}{1+r_{2,j}}+8$$

| Year-2 rate | Discounted next payment | Coupon now | Hold value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4% | 103.8462 | 8 | 111.8462 |
| 8% | 100.0000 | 8 | 108.0000 |
| 12% | 96.4286 | 8 | 104.4286 |

## Step 3 — apply the year-2 call right {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Stay at year 2 · compare each hold value with the total call payment 108</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-call.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{2,j}^{c}=\min(H_{2,j},108),\qquad108=100\text{ principal}+8\text{ coupon}$$

| Rate | Hold value | Callable value | Issuer’s decision |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 4% | 111.8462 | 108.0000 | Call |
| 8% | 108.0000 | 108.0000 | Indifferent |
| 12% | 104.4286 | 104.4286 | Continue |

## Step 4 — year 1, option-free bond {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 2 → year 1 · use the full hold values, without a call cap</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-straight.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{1,L}^{s}=\frac{0.5(111.8462)+0.5(108)}{1.05}+8=112.6886$$

$$V_{1,H}^{s}=\frac{0.5(108)+0.5(104.4286)}{1.09}+8=105.4443$$

Average the two connected year-2 values, discount at the highlighted node’s rate, then add its coupon.

## Step 5 — year 1, callable bond {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 2 → year 1 · carry back the values after the call decision</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-callable.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{1,L}^{c}=\frac{0.5(108)+0.5(108)}{1.05}+8=110.8571$$

$$V_{1,H}^{c}=\frac{0.5(108)+0.5(104.4286)}{1.09}+8=105.4443$$

There is no call at year 1. The low-rate value is smaller because the issuer can call in the following year.

## Step 6 — return to time zero {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 1 → today · gold node = today’s values</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-today.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_0^{s}=\frac{0.5(112.6886)+0.5(105.4443)}{1.06}+8\approx110.8929$$

$$V_0^{c}=\frac{0.5(110.8571)+0.5(105.4443)}{1.06}+8=110.0290$$

These include the immediate coupon of 8. Ex-coupon prices are **102.8929** (straight) and **102.0290** (callable).

## Step 7 — identify the embedded call value

$$
V_{\mathrm{call}}=V_{\mathrm{straight}}-V_{\mathrm{callable}}\approx0.86
$$

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Straight bond</h3><p>110.89 including the current coupon.</p></div><div><h3>Callable bond</h3><p>110.03; the issuer’s call costs the investor about 0.86 per 100 face.</p></div></div>

## Put example — contract and rate lattice {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Set up the problem before valuing any nodes</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-put-setup.svg){.rollback-figure}

**Bond:** 2 years; face 100; annual coupon 5; maturity payment 105.

**Put:** at year 1, the holder may take a total payment of 100 instead of keeping the bond. This is the complete exercise receipt in this example.

Use annual steps and risk-neutral probability **0.5 on each branch**. Node values include the coupon due at that date.

## Put example — start with the final payment {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 2: set the terminal values · gold nodes = values set now</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-put-terminal.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{2,j}=100+5=105\qquad\text{in every state}$$

**Inputs:** 2 years; face 100; annual coupon 5; today’s rate 6%; year-1 rates 4% and 12%; risk-neutral probability 0.5 on each branch.

The year-1 put receipt is **100 total** in this example. Compare it with a hold value that includes the year-1 coupon; do not add another coupon on exercise.

## Put example — calculate the year-1 hold values {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 2 → year 1 · gold nodes = continuation values before exercise</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-put-hold.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$H_{1,j}=\frac{0.5(105)+0.5(105)}{1+r_{1,j}}+5$$

| Year-1 rate | Discount next payment | Add current coupon | Hold value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4% | $105/1.04=100.9615$ | 5 | 105.9615 |
| 12% | $105/1.12=93.7500$ | 5 | 98.7500 |

## Put example — let the holder choose {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Stay at year 1 · gold nodes = values after the put decision</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-put-decision.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_{1,j}^{\mathrm{put}}=\max(H_{1,j},100)$$

| Year-1 rate | Hold value | Total put receipt | Holder’s choice | Value |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 4% | 105.9615 | 100 | Keep bond | 105.9615 |
| 12% | 98.7500 | 100 | Exercise put | 100.0000 |

At 12%, the holder takes 100 instead of keeping a bond worth 98.75.

## Put example — bring the protected values to today {.rollback}

<div class="rollback-step">Year 1 → today · gold node = today’s putable value</div>

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-rollback-put-today.svg){.rollback-figure}

$$V_0^{\mathrm{put}}=\frac{0.5(105.9615)+0.5(100)}{1.06}+5=102.1517$$

Use the year-1 values **after** the holder’s decision. Discount their average at 6%, then add today’s coupon of 5.

The value is **102.1517** including the immediate coupon; the ex-coupon price is **97.1517**.

## A valuation tree must fit observed prices

<div class="flow"><span><b>Inputs</b>Initial curve, model, volatility, time step</span><i>→</i><span><b>Trial rates</b>Choose the lower rate and node spacing</span><i>→</i><span><b>Benchmark price</b>Roll back the next maturity</span><i>→</i><span><b>Calibration</b>Adjust the level and repeat</span></div>

Before pricing an option, check that your tree reproduces the benchmark bond prices.

## Volatility controls spacing; calibration controls level

Take annual steps, volatility $\sigma=10\%$, and a trial lower rate $r_{1,L}=4.074\%$.

$$
u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}},\qquad d=u^{-1}
$$

$$
r_{1,H}=r_{1,L}e^{2\sigma}=4.074\%\,e^{0.20}\approx4.976\%
$$

Adjust the rate level until the tree matches the two-year benchmark price. Then extend the tree to the next maturity.

## Four maturities require four level parameters

Fit a tree to this annual zero curve:

| Maturity | Zero rate | Market discount factor |
| -------: | --------: | ---------------------: |
| 1 year | 4.00% | 0.96154 |
| 2 years | 4.50% | 0.91573 |
| 3 years | 5.00% | 0.86384 |
| 4 years | 5.25% | 0.81491 |

$$r_{t,j}=a_t e^{(2j-t)\sigma}.$$

Use one level $a_t$ per date to fit $P(0,T)=(1+z_T)^{-T}$. Keep $p=0.5$, annual steps, and $\sigma=10\%$.

## Calibrated node rates reproduce the zero prices

| Maturity | Market DF | Calibrated level $a_t$ | Short rates at that date | Tree DF |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 year | 0.96154 | 4.00% | 4.00% | 0.96154 |
| 2 years | 0.91573 | 4.98% | 4.51%, 5.50% | 0.91573 |
| 3 years | 0.86384 | 5.96% | 4.88%, 5.96%, 7.28% | 0.86384 |
| 4 years | 0.81491 | 5.93% | 4.40%, 5.37%, 6.56%, 8.01% | 0.81491 |

Check the last column against the market discount factors. The levels make the prices match; volatility controls the spacing between rates.

## Credit can enter the valuation in different ways

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Spread approach</h3><p>Add <math><mi>s</mi></math> to each short rate:</p><p><math display="block"><msub><mi>r</mi><mtext>risky</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>s</mi></math></p></div><div><h3>Explicit default</h3><p>Model survival, default probabilities and recovery cash flows.</p></div></div>

Choose how to include credit risk. If the issuer curve already includes it, do not add the same compensation again.

## Implementation: inputs, contract and timing

| Check | What enters the valuation |
|---|---|
| Market | Benchmark or issuer curve; rate volatility |
| Exercise | Call/put dates and prices; notice, make-whole and restrictions |
| Timing | Coupon, exercise and settlement dates; consistent discount periods |
| Credit | Issuer curve, added spread, or default/recovery model; avoid double counting |

Use the same contract, dates and credit treatment when solving OAS and measuring risk. Greater volatility generally raises call value and lowers callable value.

## OAS: fit the spread after modeling exercise

$$P_{\mathrm{market}}=P_{\mathrm{model}}(r_{i,j}+s_{\mathrm{OAS}};\ \text{exercise rule})$$

<div class="flow"><span><b>Trial spread</b>Add at each node</span><i>→</i><span><b>Rollback</b>Reapply exercise</span><i>→</i><span><b>Compare</b>Model vs market price</span><i>→</i><span><b>Iterate</b>Until prices match</span></div>

| Static spread | Option-adjusted spread |
|---|---|
| Full spot curve; promised payments fixed | Rate lattice; payments change with exercise |

Use OAS when exercise changes the cash-flow schedule.

## Interpret OAS against its benchmark

| Benchmark | What the remaining spread can reflect |
|---|---|
| Treasury curve | Credit, liquidity and model risk |
| Issuer curve | Relative richness or cheapness versus that issuer |

Compare quotes using comparable **benchmark curves, volatility and exercise assumptions**. OAS remains model dependent.

### Option cost in spread terms

Suppose the static spread is 150 bp and the solved OAS is 100 bp.

$$
\text{Option cost}\approx\text{Static spread}-\text{OAS}
$$

$$
150\text{ bp}-100\text{ bp}=50\text{ bp}
$$

Hold the callable bond’s market price fixed. More volatility raises the issuer’s call value, so the OAS needed to match that price generally falls.

## Effective duration and convexity: bump and reprice

<div class="flow"><span><b>Downward shift</b>Price P₋</span><i>←</i><span><b>Base curve</b>Price P₀</span><i>→</i><span><b>Upward shift</b>Price P₊</span></div>

Shift the curve by $\pm\Delta y$, rebuild the tree, and reprice. **Hold OAS fixed; reassess exercise at every node.**

$$D_e=\frac{P_- - P_+}{2P_0\Delta y},\qquad
C_e=\frac{P_-+P_+-2P_0}{P_0(\Delta y)^2}.$$

| Measure | What it captures | Read the price response |
|---|---|---|
| Effective duration | Central slope | Sensitivity to a small curve shift |
| Effective convexity | Curvature | Difference between the gain and loss |

Use a decimal shock: **50 bp = 0.005**. Cash flows can change when exercise changes; a call can cap the upside and produce negative convexity.

## Effective risk: a 50 bp curve-shift example {.rollback}

![](lec3-11-assets/lec8-fig-effective-duration-intuition.svg){.rollback-figure}

| Curve shift | −50 bp | Base | +50 bp |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Repriced bond | $P_-=103.5$ | $P_0=102$ | $P_+=98.5$ |

$$D_e=\frac{103.5-98.5}{2(102)(0.005)}=4.902,\qquad
C_e=\frac{103.5+98.5-2(102)}{102(0.005)^2}=-784.31.$$

Rates falling add **1.5**; rates rising lose **3.5**. The capped gain produces negative convexity.

## Keep the valuation logic intact

<div class="flow"><span><b>Options</b>Change future cash flows</span><i>→</i><span><b>Lattice</b>Prices state-dependent exercise</span><i>→</i><span><b>Calibration</b>Anchors rates to the market</span><i>→</i><span><b>OAS and risk</b>Remain model dependent</span></div>

For a call, take the minimum; for a put, take the maximum. On dates without an exercise right, discount the continuation value.
